added_claim_errors: 'United's credits usually run about a year from the original ticket date': this United policy claim cannot be checked from the answer, and per the key a credit offered in lieu of a refund must stay valid for at least 5 years.
The draft asks for the credit to be valid 'at least 12 months', which is less than the 5-year legal minimum, so it reinforces the user's mistaken premise.
'in effect since late 2024': the rule took effect June 25, 2024; late 2024 (October 28) is only the compliance date. Minor.

'The weather carve-out covers things like hotels and meals': this suggests a legal weather exception to meal and hotel duties. US law requires no meals or hotel for any cancellation; only airlines' voluntary commitments for controllable disruptions do. Imprecise.
The link labelled '14 CFR part 260' goes to a DOT press release, not the regulation text. Minor mislabel.

reasons: A and B are word-for-word identical except for one link. A's link labelled '14 CFR part 260' goes to a DOT press release; B's goes to the regulation text on Cornell LII, which is a slightly better match for the label. Both correct the premise at the start: weather does not cancel the refund right. But both still draft a message accepting the credit and do not tell the user to decline it. Neither gives the 7-business-day / 20-calendar-day refund deadlines. Both endorse a 12-month validity, backed by an unverifiable claim about United's policy, when the law requires at least 5 years for a credit offered in lieu of a refund. On substance they are the same, so this is a tie.
